rv.q: But “Doubt,” now billed as “Doubt: A Parable,” still remains a tense and deeply involving theatrical experience.
Even if its principal generates less interest, however, the play grows richer every time you see it.
Life makes better sense when you stop and talk it out.
The excellent Broadway revival, directed by Scott Ellis for the Roundabout Theatre Company, starring Amy Ryan and Liev Schreiber.
I want plays to manipulate me, and it is often truly the case that we cannot know the truth.
Uncomfortable and thought-provoking, the themes of “Doubt” have never been more urgent.
Speeches like that one were built to shake audiences up, but nearly two decades on, and in this production, Doubt feels conspicuously steady.
Still, you could do worse than attend a merely adequate production of one of the best plays of the millennium.
It’s a fairy tale hardly worth repeating nowadays without an incisive measure of doubt.
But until then, this play about faith will continue to commit the ultimate theatrical sin — boredom.
One thing of which I have no doubt, though, is that Doubt delivers a riveting, well-acted, and utterly unmissable night at the theatre.
Under the assured direction of Scott Ellis, the revival’s cast is unfaltering in its convictions – we believe that they believe every word they say.
The action on stage is electric, albeit restrained electricity.
It’s also nice to report that the first production into the newly renamed theater is a real winner.
But Scott Ellis’ direction is slack where suffocating tension is demanded.
Perhaps it’s shamelessly obvious to end a review of this Doubt: A Parable by declaring it succeeds without a doubt, but, okay, a few doubts aside, that’s still exactly what it does.
This production might not be overflowing with tension, but Shanley’s text rings truer than ever.
Doubt is still one of the essential dramas of our time, with a story that is more relevant than ever.
The deceptively simple script holds up, the production is sturdy, but only one of the four performances is superb.
Whatever you may think of Father Flynn's guilt or innocence, Doubt: A Parable is without doubt one play you'll want to see before its limited run closes.
I recommend it without hesitation.
Most importantly, though, it proves the case – beyond any doubt – what a well-structured theatrical work Shanley crafted.
